idiom_name: module boundary + pure mapping functions + schema validation at the seam (zod/AJV)
implementation_notes: JavaScript's boundary is the module: an acl/ folder whose index re-exports domain-shaped functions (placeOrder(order) -> receipt) while its internals are the only code importing the vendor SDK or calling fetch; translation is a few pure functions with explicit field mapping, and because nothing is typed at run time the seam must validate - a schema (zod, AJV) parses the foreign payload before it is mapped, which is the JS substitute for a compiler-enforced boundary. What replaces the facade/adapter/translator classes is that module boundary plus the parse-then-map discipline; explicit classes are still justified when the adapter holds configuration, several methods, or must be injected for tests.
pitfalls: Without runtime validation the layer only renames data: an upstream field change becomes a silent undefined deep in the domain, since JS has no compiler to catch it.
CommonJS/ESM interop: importing the vendor's CJS build into an ESM boundary can instantiate a second copy of the SDK (dual-package hazard); keep the vendor call in one module.
Floating promises and unhandled rejections in the adapter escape the domain's error contract - await and translate explicitly.
A module boundary is convention, not enforcement: a lint rule (no-restricted-imports) or dependency check is what keeps the vendor SDK out of the rest of the app.
